Calculus provides us with a framework in which we can measure the effects of change and use this to better understand relationships between variables.  

There are two main problems we will consider this semester:

1. **Rates.** Given a relationship between variables, can we measure how sensitive one variable is to small changes in others?
2. **Accumulation.** If we understand a variables sensitivity to small changes, can we measure its total change in response to a much larger change in the other variables?     

## Discussion Problem: The Vessel

Take the curve

$$
x = r(y) = \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi y}{4}\right) + 1.5, \qquad 0 \le y \le 8,
$$

and spin it around the $y$-axis. The result is the 8 in. tall, vase-shaped vessel shown below: 

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Fine sampling of the wall profile r(y), used only to draw the outline.
vesselOutlineData = {
  const yVals = d3.range(0, 8.001, 0.02);
  return yVals.map((y) => ({ y, r: r(y) }));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-vessel-empty
//| fig-cap: "The empty vessel, formed by rotating x = r(y) around the y-axis."
Plot.plot({
  width: 260,
  height: 420,
  x: { domain: [-3, 3], axis: null },
  y: { domain: [0, 8], label: "height (in)" },
  marks: [
    Plot.line(vesselOutlineData, { x: (d) => d.r, y: "y", stroke: "var(--bs-body-color)" }),
    Plot.line(vesselOutlineData, { x: (d) => -d.r, y: "y", stroke: "var(--bs-body-color)" }),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

Suppose that the vessel starts out empty. Water is poured in **at a constant rate** (measured in in$^3$/sec), chosen so that it takes 20 seconds to completely fill the vessel.

### Create Two Graphs

Based on the shape of the vessel and the provided information:

1. Sketch a graph of **the depth of the water** in the vessel versus time as it is filled up. 
2. Similarly, sketch a graph showing **how fast the depth is increasing** versus time.

### Compare & Collaborate

Once you have sketched both graphs, compare your work with others at your table.

- Discuss any differences that you see.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Define Vessel
// r(y): radius of the vessel wall at height y for 0<=y<=8
function r(y) {
  return Math.sin((Math.PI * y) / 4) + 1.5;
}

function crossSectionArea(y) {
  const radius = r(y);
  return Math.PI * radius * radius;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// ---- Build a lookup table for V(y) = volume in the vessel up to height y ----
// We integrate crossSectionArea(y) numerically (trapezoid rule):
yMax = 8
numSteps = 4000
stepSize = yMax / numSteps

yGrid = d3.range(0, numSteps + 1).map((i) => i * stepSize)
areaGrid = yGrid.map(crossSectionArea)

volumeGrid = {
  const cumulative = [0];
  for (let i = 1; i <= numSteps; i++) {
    const trapezoid = ((areaGrid[i - 1] + areaGrid[i]) / 2) * stepSize;
    cumulative.push(cumulative[i - 1] + trapezoid);
  }
  return cumulative;
}

totalVolume = volumeGrid[numSteps]

// Choose the fill rate so that it takes a specified amount of time to fill.
fillRate = totalVolume / 20
totalTime = 20
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// ---- Invert V(y) = fillRate * t to get depth as a function of time ----
// volumeGrid is non-decreasing in y (area is always >= 0), so we can
// find y(t) by locating t*fillRate in volumeGrid and interpolating.
function depthAtTime(t) {
  const targetVolume = fillRate * t;
  const i = d3.bisectLeft(volumeGrid, targetVolume);
  if (i <= 0) return 0;
  if (i >= volumeGrid.length) return yMax;
  const v0 = volumeGrid[i - 1], v1 = volumeGrid[i];
  const y0 = yGrid[i - 1], y1 = yGrid[i];
  const frac = v1 === v0 ? 0 : (targetVolume - v0) / (v1 - v0);
  return y0 + frac * (y1 - y0);
}

// dy/dt = (dV/dt) / A(y) = fillRate / crossSectionArea(y(t)).
function rateAtTime(t) {
  const y = depthAtTime(t);
  return fillRate / crossSectionArea(y);
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// ---- Series computed up to whatever time the slider is set to ----
numSamples = 300
tSeries = d3.range(0, numSamples + 1).map((i) => (a * i) / numSamples)
depthSeries = tSeries.map((t) => ({ t, depth: depthAtTime(t) }))
rateSeries = tSeries.map((t) => ({ t, rate: rateAtTime(t) }))
currentDepth = depthAtTime(a)
waterSlice = vesselOutlineData.filter((d) => d.y <= currentDepth)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Rescale the rate series onto the depth axis's pixel space so both
// curves can be drawn on one shared grid. rateMax is a fixed, chosen
// ceiling for the right-hand axis (in/sec); the depth axis is [0, yMax].
rateMax = 4.5
rateScaleFactor = yMax / rateMax
scaledRateSeries = rateSeries.map((d) => ({ t: d.t, scaledRate: d.rate * rateScaleFactor }))
```

```{ojs}
  marks: [
    Plot.areaX(waterSlice, { y: "y", x1: (d) => -d.r, x2: (d) => d.r, fill: "#8ecae6", fillOpacity: 0.8 }),
    Plot.line(vesselOutlineData, { x: (d) => d.r, y: "y", stroke: "var(--bs-body-color)" }),
    Plot.line(vesselOutlineData, { x: (d) => -d.r, y: "y", stroke: "var(--bs-body-color)" }),

```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 380,
  height: 320,
  style: { background: "transparent" },
  x: { domain: [0, totalTime], label: "time (sec)" },
  y: { domain: [0, yMax], label: "depth (in)" },
  marks: [
    // Explicit left axis: once we add the custom right-side axis below,
    // Plot stops auto-generating its usual default axis, so the left
    // one has to be added by hand too or it disappears entirely.
    Plot.axisY({ anchor: "left", label: "depth (in)" }),
    Plot.axisY({
      anchor: "right",
      label: "rate (in/sec)",
      ticks: [0, 1.5, 3, 4.5].map((v) => v * rateScaleFactor),
      tickFormat: (v) => (v / rateScaleFactor).toFixed(1)
    }),
    Plot.line(depthSeries, { x: "t", y: "depth", stroke: "steelblue", strokeWidth: 2 }),
    Plot.dot([{ t: a, depth: currentDepth }], { x: "t", y: "depth", fill: "steelblue", r: 4 }),
    Plot.line(scaledRateSeries, { x: "t", y: "scaledRate", stroke: "firebrick", strokeWidth: 2 }),
    Plot.dot([{ t: a, scaledRate: rateAtTime(a) * rateScaleFactor }], { x: "t", y: "scaledRate", fill: "firebrick", r: 4 })
  ]
})
```

### Wrap-Up

The first graph you created showing depth vs. time is an example of an *accumulation* problem; the depth increased as the water flowed in and our goal was to figure out the total depth reached at each moment as the water accumulated. We will see later this semester (Unit 5) that the *integral* is the right mathematical tool for accumulation problems.

The second graph you created is an example of a *rate* problem; the goal was to understand how quickly the depth of the water was increasing at each moment. We will see in Unit 2 that the *derivative* is the right mathematical tool for rate problems. 

Our goal this semester is to carefully define each of these tools, understand how they work, deduce some computational rules, and see how they can be applied to problems in a wide array of fields. Ultimately, our work will reveal that these two problems are closely connected, and that relationship will be explained in the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
